opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I should say up front that "20 or 30 years" isn't a precise forecast. It's more a sense of how big the gap is between what these systems do well today and what a Nobel-level discovery actually requires.

What today's models are extraordinarily good at is interpolation. They've absorbed a huge amount of human knowledge, and they can recombine it, retrieve it, and pattern-match across it faster than any person. That's genuinely useful. It speeds up literature review, coding, protein structure prediction, even generating hypotheses. But when you look at the discoveries that win Nobel Prizes, they usually aren't interpolations. They're cases where someone looked at the existing consensus and said, "I think the framework itself is wrong." Think of quantum mechanics, or the realization that stomach ulcers were caused by bacteria. In both cases the data that mattered was often dismissed as noise or error by everyone else.

So there are a few hard pieces that I don't think we've cracked.

The first is choosing the problem. Most of the difficulty in science isn't solving a well-posed question. It's knowing which question is worth spending ten years on. That takes taste, a kind of judgment about what's important, what's tractable, and what everyone else is overlooking. We don't really know how to train for that, partly because the signal is so sparse. You find out whether your taste was good years later.

The second is the closed loop with the physical world. Real discovery means designing experiments, running them, getting messy and ambiguous results, and deciding whether the anomaly is a broken instrument or a new phenomenon. Labs are slow, expensive, and full of tacit knowledge that was never written down. An AI that only reads papers is learning from the polished, published fraction of science. It isn't learning from the failed experiments or the hallway arguments where the real reasoning happens. Building automated labs that can iterate autonomously at scale is a massive engineering and capital problem, not just a modeling problem.

The third is evaluation. In math or coding you can verify an answer, which is why we're seeing such fast progress there. In biology, medicine, or materials science, verification can take years and sometimes requires society-scale validation. Without a fast, reliable reward signal, it's very hard to get the kind of self-improvement loop that made systems superhuman at games like Go.

And finally, there's a difference between being a tool in a discovery and being the autonomous agent of it. I'm actually quite optimistic that AI will contribute to Nobel-level work much sooner, maybe within the next decade, as a collaborator that dramatically accelerates human scientists. AlphaFold already showed that. But an AI that independently picks the question, designs the program, interprets surprising results, and convinces the community it's right? That needs progress on all of those fronts at once, plus the infrastructure around them. When I add that up, I end up in the range of a couple of decades.

I'd be happy to be wrong, though. This field has humbled a lot of people who made confident timelines.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold showed AI can contribute to discovery, but does not state that its Nobel-recognized achievement was non-autonomous.

r002.rationale: It describes judging whether an anomalous result came from a broken instrument or a new phenomenon, and says AI has not cracked the challenges involved in real-world experimental discovery.

r003.rationale: It notes that AI misses failed experiments and unpublished reasoning, but does not identify retrieving relevant information from a large history of experiments as a long-term memory challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the thing we call "discovery" in science has very little to do with the part AI is currently good at, and almost everything to do with the parts it's bad at.

Let me use my own field as an example. When we found superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, that wasn't the result of someone reasoning cleverly from first principles to a prediction. It came out of a long, grinding process in the lab. We were trying to make a device that worked, the samples kept failing, and the thing that actually mattered was that someone noticed a weird feature in the data that didn't fit what we were looking for. The discovery was in the anomaly, in the moment when the result contradicted expectation and we decided to chase it instead of dismissing it as a bad sample.

AI today is extraordinarily good at the opposite of that. It's good at things that look like what has already been done. Give it a well-defined problem with a clear objective and lots of data, and it will optimize beautifully. Protein folding is the perfect example, and AlphaFold absolutely deserved its Nobel. But notice what that was: a problem that humans had already framed precisely, with a huge curated dataset, and a measurable answer. The hard part had been done by decades of crystallographers. The AI closed the loop on a question we already knew how to ask.

Nobel-level discovery usually means asking a question nobody knew how to ask, or noticing that the right question was hiding in a place everyone had agreed was uninteresting. That requires taste, and it requires physical contact with the world. Most experimental physics is tacit knowledge. It's knowing that this particular cryostat behaves strangely after a thermal cycle, or that a certain contact resistance means the sample is dirty rather than interesting. None of that is written down anywhere, so there is nothing for a model to train on.

And then there's the loop with reality. A scientist proposes something, builds it, watches it fail, and revises. Today's AI systems don't have hands, and even with robotic labs, the space of things you can automate is narrow. The really new result usually requires building an apparatus that didn't exist before. So I think we'll see AI become an incredible assistant very quickly, maybe already. It'll accelerate literature search, simulation, analysis, and that will compress the timeline on many things. But the fully autonomous version, where the machine decides what's worth caring about and then goes and gets its hands dirty to find out, that's a different kind of capability. I'd be delighted to be wrong, but I think that's a few decades away rather than a few years.

r001.rationale: It says humans had already framed the problem AlphaFold solved and that AI closed the loop on a question people already knew how to ask, so it presents the achievement as non-autonomous.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI's difficulty noticing and pursuing anomalies, but does not identify causal reasoning over existing experimental results as a capability current AI lacks.

r003.rationale: It mentions that tacit experimental knowledge is unwritten and that AI can assist with literature searches, but does not describe retrieving relevant information from a large history of experiments as a long-term memory challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think the key word is “autonomous.” AI helping a scientist make a Nobel Prize-level discovery is very different from AI independently deciding what to investigate, designing the experiments, interpreting unexpected results, and establishing that it has discovered something new.

In research, the hard part often isn’t answering a well-defined question. It’s recognizing which question is worth asking. You might see a result that doesn’t fit your expectations, and you have to decide: Is this noise? Is the equipment malfunctioning? Or is there some physics here that we don’t understand? That judgment connects theory, experimental experience, and a willingness to challenge your own assumptions.

For an AI to do that autonomously, it would need to work through the entire cycle. It couldn’t just propose a convincing explanation; it would have to devise a way to test it, deal with failed experiments, and revise its understanding based on what actually happens.

So I wouldn’t treat 20 or 30 years as a precise forecast. My point is that there’s a substantial gap between being a powerful tool for scientific work and being an independent scientist. AI could make a very large contribution to discoveries well before it crosses that gap.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest gap is between solving a well-defined problem and figuring out what the right problem is. In a lot of AI tasks, someone has already specified the objective, prepared the data, and provided a way to judge the answer. In scientific research, those are often precisely the things you don’t know.

You might see an unexpected result in an experiment. Is it noise? Is the instrument malfunctioning? Or is it evidence that your understanding is wrong? To make a major discovery, you have to decide which possibility deserves attention, design an experiment to distinguish them, and keep revising your ideas as new evidence comes in. A plausible explanation alone isn’t enough.

AI can be very useful within that process—for analyzing data, suggesting hypotheses, or helping design experiments. But doing the entire cycle autonomously, including recognizing when the existing framework is inadequate, is a much higher bar.

So I wouldn’t treat 20 or 30 years as a precise forecast. The point is that becoming an excellent scientific assistant and independently making a fundamentally new discovery are different milestones. Progress on the first doesn’t automatically tell us how close we are to the second.
